claim: RE neurons form synapses in the stratum oriens (SO) and lacunosum-moleculare (SLM) of the dCA1 area, but not in the stratum radiatum (SR).
source: Anatomical tracing and chemogenetic manipulation in mice demonstrate that RE neurons form synapses and regulate synaptic transmission in the stratum oriens (SO) and lacunosum-moleculare (SLM) of the dCA1 area, but not in the stratum radiatum (SR).
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical tracing data showing RE axons and boutons in SO and SLM (Figure 1), and electrophysiological recordings showing CNO decreased fEPSP in SO and SLM but not SR (Figure 1J-L).

claim: RE neurons regulate synaptic transmission in the stratum oriens (SO) and lacunosum-moleculare (SLM) of the dCA1 area, but not in the stratum radiatum (SR).
source: Anatomical tracing and chemogenetic manipulation in mice demonstrate that RE neurons form synapses and regulate synaptic transmission in the stratum oriens (SO) and lacunosum-moleculare (SLM) of the dCA1 area, but not in the stratum radiatum (SR).
evidence: Chemogenetic inhibition of RE→dCA1 neurons decreased fEPSP in SO and SLM but not SR, as shown in Figure 1J-L.

claim: CFE induces structural changes of excitatory synapses in both SO and SLM strata innervated by RE, but not in SR.
source: We also observe CFE-specific structural changes of excitatory synapses and expression of the synaptic scaffold protein, PSD-95, in both strata innervated by RE, but not in SR.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data showing changes in dendritic spine morphology and PSD-95 levels in SO and SLM but not SR after CFE (Figure 3).

claim: CFE induces changes in PSD-95 expression in both SO and SLM strata innervated by RE, but not in SR.
source: We also observe CFE-specific structural changes of excitatory synapses and expression of the synaptic scaffold protein, PSD-95, in both strata innervated by RE, but not in SR.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data showing altered PSD-95 levels per dendritic spine in SO and SLM but not SR after CFE (Figure 3).

claim: Only the changes in SLM are specific for the dendrites innervated by RE.
source: Interestingly, only the changes in SLM are specific for the dendrites innervated by RE.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis showing that CFE-induced changes in dendritic spine area and PSD-95 levels occurred on RE+ dendrites in SLM but on RE- dendrites in SO (Figure 3).

claim: Brief chemogenetic inhibition of the RE→dCA1 pathway during a CFE session persistently impairs the formation of CFE memory.
source: To further support the role of the RE→dCA1 projection in CFE, we demonstrate that brief chemogenetic inhibition of the RE→dCA1 pathway during a CFE session persistently impairs the formation of CFE memory and CFE-induced changes of PSD-95 levels in SLM.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data showing that CNO-mediated inhibition of RE→dCA1 during extinction resulted in higher freezing levels during subsequent tests (Figure 6D, F, G).

claim: Brief chemogenetic inhibition of the RE→dCA1 pathway during a CFE session impairs CFE-induced changes of PSD-95 levels in SLM.
source: To further support the role of the RE→dCA1 projection in CFE, we demonstrate that brief chemogenetic inhibition of the RE→dCA1 pathway during a CFE session persistently impairs the formation of CFE memory and CFE-induced changes of PSD-95 levels in SLM.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data showing that CNO treatment in hM4Di mice reduced PSD-95 levels in SLM compared to controls (Figure 7D).

claim: RE participates in CFE by regulating CFE-induced molecular remodeling of dCA1 synapses.
source: Thus, our data indicate that RE participates in CFE by regulating CFE-induced molecular remodeling of dCA1 synapses.
evidence: The claim is supported by data showing that RE inhibition blocks CFE-induced PSD-95 changes (Figure 7) and impairs CFE memory (Figure 6), combined with anatomical evidence of RE→dCA1 synaptic changes during CFE (Figures 2-5).

claim: mCherry was expressed in more than 60% of RE cells spreading from Bregma –0.46 mm to –1.5 mm.
source: AAV2.1:camk2a_mCherry) (Figure 1A), resulting in mCherry expression in more than 60% of RE cells spreading from Bregma –0.46 mm to –1.5 mm (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of viral expression shown in Figure 1B.

claim: RE axons labeled by mCherry were analyzed in the SO, SLM, and SR of dCA1.
source: RE axons labeled by mCherry were analyzed in the SO, SLM, and SR of dCA1 (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy images and quantification shown in Figure 1C-G.

claim: 21 tissue bricks (67.7 × 67.7 × 5.4 μm) per stratum were analyzed, containing on average 37 μm of axons per tissue bricks in SO, 0.7 μm in SR, and 65 μm in SLM.
source: We analyzed 21 tissue bricks (67.7 × 67.7 × 5.4 μm) per stratum, containing on average 37 μm of axons per tissue bricks in SO, 0.7 μm in SR, and 65 μm in SLM.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of axon length shown in Figure 1E.

claim: RE boutons were identified in SO and SLM as axonal thickenings in close apposition to PSD-95-positive puncta.
source: RE boutons were identified in SO and SLM as axonal thickenings in close apposition to PSD-95-positive puncta (a synaptic scaffold used as a marker of excitatory synapses that can be located both on excitatory and inhibitory neurons; Chen et al., 2011; El-Husseini et al., 2000; Kornau et al., 1995; Dharmasri et al., 2024; Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy images showing colocalization of mCherry-labeled axons with PSD-95 immunostaining (Figure 1D), and is based on established knowledge about PSD-95 as a synaptic marker.

claim: Density of RE boutons in SLM was slightly lower compared to SO boutons.
source: Density of RE boutons in SLM was slightly lower, and boutons were much larger, compared to SO boutons (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 1F (Mann–Whitney test, U = 108, p=0.060).

claim: RE boutons in SLM were much larger compared to SO boutons.
source: Density of RE boutons in SLM was slightly lower, and boutons were much larger, compared to SO boutons (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 1G (Mann–Whitney test, U = 12,550. p<0.001).

claim: CNO decreased fEPSP in SLM.
source: CNO decreased fEPSP in SLM (RM ANOVA, effect of CNO, F(1, 24)=4.95, p=0.036)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1L.

claim: CNO decreased fEPSP in SO.
source: CNO decreased fEPSP in SLM (RM ANOVA, effect of CNO, F(1, 24)=4.95, p=0.036) and SO (F(1, 16)=5.906, p=0.027)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1J.

claim: CNO did not decrease fEPSP in SR.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1K.

claim: CNO slightly decreased FV amplitudes in SLM.
source: CNO slightly decreased FV amplitudes in SLM (RM two-way ANOVA, F(1, 19)=3.752, p=0.068)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1L.

claim: CNO did not decrease FV amplitudes in SO.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1J.

claim: CNO did not decrease FV amplitudes in SR.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 1K.

claim: RE innervates and efficiently regulates excitatory synaptic transmission in SLM and SO.
source: Hence, our data indicate that RE innervates and efficiently regulates excitatory synaptic transmission in SLM and SO.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the anatomical data showing RE axons in SO and SLM (Figure 1C-G) and electrophysiological data showing CNO-mediated reduction of fEPSP in these strata (Figure 1J, L).

claim: dCA1, RE, as well as RE→dCA1 projections have been implicated in the extinction of contextual fear.
source: dCA1, RE, as well as RE→dCA1 projections have been implicated in the extinction of contextual fear (Venkataraman and Dias, 2023; Cassel et al., 2013; Totty et al., 2023; Ratigan et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Extinction of contextual fear remodels dendritic spines specifically in SO and SLM of dCA1.
source: Moreover, our recent study showed that the extinction of contextual fear remodels dendritic spines specifically in SO and SLM of dCA1 (Ziółkowska et al., 2023), two strata innervated by RE (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the same authors.

claim: At the beginning of the CFC, freezing levels were low but increased during the training.
source: At the beginning of the CFC, freezing levels were low but increased during the training.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: At the beginning of the CFE session, freezing levels were high, indicating contextual fear memory.
source: At the beginning of the CFE session, freezing levels were high, indicating contextual fear memory, and decreased within the session, indicating formation of CFE memory (Figure 2A; Ziółkowska et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Freezing levels decreased within the CFE session, indicating formation of CFE memory.
source: At the beginning of the CFE session, freezing levels were high, indicating contextual fear memory, and decreased within the session, indicating formation of CFE memory (Figure 2A; Ziółkowska et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: mCherry was expressed in over 68% of RE cells.
source: Post-training analysis of the brain sections showed that mCherry was expressed in RE, the levels of AAV transduction did not differ between the experimental groups, and was observed in over 68% of RE cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of viral expression shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The levels of AAV transduction did not differ between the experimental groups.
source: Post-training analysis of the brain sections showed that mCherry was expressed in RE, the levels of AAV transduction did not differ between the experimental groups, and was observed in over 68% of RE cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The analysis of the presynaptic boutons in SO revealed no significant differences in density and size between the experimental groups.
source: The analysis of the presynaptic boutons in SO revealed no significant differences in density and size between the experimental groups (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The density of RE boutons in SLM did not differ between the experimental groups.
source: Similarly in SLM, the density of RE boutons did not differ between the experimental groups.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The Ext mice had significantly larger RE boutons compared to the 5US animals.
source: However, the Ext mice had significantly larger RE boutons compared to the 5US animals, and no difference was observed between the Ext and Naive mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2D (Mann–Whitney test, U = 29409; p<0.001).

claim: No difference in RE bouton size was observed between the Ext and Naive mice.
source: However, the Ext mice had significantly larger RE boutons compared to the 5US animals, and no difference was observed between the Ext and Naive mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Behavioral training did not affect RE→SO presynapses.
source: Hence, our data suggest that the behavioral training did not affect RE→SO presynapses, while CFC decreased the size of RE→SLM pre-synapses and this process was reversed by CFE.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of significant differences in RE bouton density and size in SO between experimental groups (Figure 2C).

claim: CFC decreased the size of RE→SLM pre-synapses and this process was reversed by CFE.
source: Hence, our data suggest that the behavioral training did not affect RE→SO presynapses, while CFC decreased the size of RE→SLM pre-synapses and this process was reversed by CFE.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that 5US mice had smaller RE boutons than Ext mice, while Ext mice did not differ from Naive mice (Figure 2D).

claim: The average length of the analyzed dendritic fragments per tissue brick (67.7 × 67.7 × 5.4 μm) was 50 μm in SO, 53 in SR, and 40 μm in SLM.
source: The average length of the analyzed dendritic fragments per tissue brick (67.7 × 67.7 × 5.4 μm) was 50 μm in SO, 53 in SR, and 40 μm in SLM.
evidence: The claim is based on measurements from confocal microscopy analysis.

claim: Analyzed dendritic fragments contained on average respectively 25, 37, and 32 dendritic spines in SO, SR, and SLM, including 1–3 RE+/+ in SO and 1–4 RE+/+ in SLM.
source: They contained on average respectively 25, 37, and 32 dendritic spines, including 1–3 RE+/+ in SO and 1–4 RE+/+ in SLM.
evidence: The claim is based on quantification from confocal microscopy analysis.

claim: The 5US animals tended to have more spines in SO compared to Naive and Ext animals.
source: However, the 5US animals tended to have more spines, and these spines were smaller and contained less PSD-95 as compared to those in the Naive and Ext animals (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C, and Supplementary file 1a–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Spines in SO of 5US animals were smaller and contained less PSD-95 compared to those in the Naive and Ext animals.
source: However, the 5US animals tended to have more spines, and these spines were smaller and contained less PSD-95 as compared to those in the Naive and Ext animals (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–C, and Supplementary file 1a–c).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Spine changes in SO were specific for the RE- dendrites.
source: Interestingly, these spine changes were specific for the RE- dendrites.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis showing that changes in spine area and PSD-95 levels occurred on RE- dendrites but not RE+/- or RE+/+ spines in SO (Figure 3B).

claim: CFE reversed synaptic changes on RE- dendrites induced by CFC in SO.
source: Hence, CFE reversed synaptic changes on RE- dendrites induced by CFC.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that Ext group did not differ from Naive but differed from 5US group in spine characteristics on RE- dendrites in SO (Figure 3B).

claim: RE+/- spines in 5US and Ext groups contained less PSD-95 compared to the Naive animals in SO.
source: However, RE+/- spines in 5US and Ext groups contained less PSD-95 compared to the Naive animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3B.

claim: No significant training-induced changes in density and size of dendritic spines were observed in SR.
source: In SR, we did not observe any significant training-induced changes in density and size of dendritic spines.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3C.

claim: PSD-95 levels per dendritic spine were decreased in the Ext and 5US groups compared to the Naive animals in SR.
source: However, PSD-95 levels per dendritic spine were decreased in the Ext and 5US groups compared to the Naive animals (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–F, and Supplementary file 1d–f).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3C.

claim: No significant changes in dendritic spine density were observed globally or on RE- dendrites in SLM.
source: In SLM, no significant changes in dendritic spine density were observed globally or on RE- dendrites; however, we found increased density of RE+/+ dendritic spines (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–I, and Supplementary file 1g–i).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Increased density of RE+/+ dendritic spines was found in SLM.
source: In SLM, no significant changes in dendritic spine density were observed globally or on RE- dendrites; however, we found increased density of RE+/+ dendritic spines (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1G–I, and Supplementary file 1g–i).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There were more RE+/+ spines in the Ext group compared to the 5US animals in SLM.
source: There were also more RE+/+ spines in the Ext group compared to the 5US animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The median dendritic spine area was higher in the Ext group compared to 5US animals in SLM, and these differences were specific for the RE+ dendrites.
source: Moreover, the median dendritic spine area and PSD-95 expression per dendritic spine were higher in the Ext group compared to 5US animals, and these differences were specific for the RE+ dendrites.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3D.

claim: PSD-95 expression per dendritic spine was higher in the Ext group compared to 5US animals in SLM, and these differences were specific for the RE+ dendrites.
source: Moreover, the median dendritic spine area and PSD-95 expression per dendritic spine were higher in the Ext group compared to 5US animals, and these differences were specific for the RE+ dendrites.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3D.

claim: No changes in spine characteristics were observed on the RE- dendrites in SLM.
source: Again, no such changes were observed on the RE- dendrites.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3D.

claim: CFE-induced growth of RE buttons in SLM matches the observed postsynaptic changes.
source: These observations match the CFE-induced growth of RE buttons in SLM (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between presynaptic (Figure 2D) and postsynaptic (Figure 3D) changes in SLM.

claim: RE+/+ dendritic spines constitute 5–6% of all synapses in dCA1.
source: Although RE+/+ dendritic spines are sparse in dCA1 (based on mCherry AAV penetrance in RE and frequency of RE+/+ dendritic spines in our study, we asses that they constitute 5–6% of all synapses)
evidence: The claim is inferred from the AAV penetrance data (68% in RE) and the frequency of RE+/+ spines observed in the study.

claim: The mice showed low levels of freezing both during the first and second exposure to the experimental context in the control experiment.
source: The mice showed low levels of freezing both during the first and second exposure to the experimental context, indicating no fear memory.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: No significant difference in AAV penetrance in RE was observed between the Ctx and Ctx-Ctx experimental groups.
source: Post-training analysis of the brain sections revealed no significant difference in AAV penetrance in RE between the experimental groups (penetrance: Ctx: 66%; Ctx-Ctx: 60%).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of viral expression.

claim: No global differences in density and size of RE boutons in SLM were observed between the Ctx and Ctx-Ctx animals.
source: We also observed no global differences in density and size of RE boutons (Figure 4B and C) and dendritic spines (Figure 4D and E) in SLM between the Ctx and Ctx-Ctx animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: No global differences in density and size of dendritic spines in SLM were observed between the Ctx and Ctx-Ctx animals.
source: We also observed no global differences in density and size of RE boutons (Figure 4B and C) and dendritic spines (Figure 4D and E) in SLM between the Ctx and Ctx-Ctx animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Synapses in all dCA1 strata undergo structural or molecular changes relevant to CFC and/or CFE.
source: Overall, our data demonstrate that synapses in all dCA1 strata undergo structural or molecular changes relevant to CFC and/or CFE.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of changes in dendritic spines and PSD-95 levels across SO, SR, and SLM (Figure 3).

claim: Only in SLM CFE-induced synaptic changes are likely to be directly regulated by RE inputs as they appear on RE+ dendrites and spines.
source: However, only in SLM CFE-induced synaptic changes are likely to be directly regulated by RE inputs as they appear on RE+ dendrites and spines.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that CFE-induced changes in SLM occurred specifically on RE+ dendrites and spines, while changes in SO occurred on RE- dendrites (Figure 3).

claim: The described structural plasticity at the RE→SLM synapses is involved in CFE, rather than in processing contextual information in general.
source: Since such changes of SLM synapses were not observed in the animals re-exposed to the neutral context, our data support the role of the described structural plasticity at the RE→SLM synapses in CFE, rather than in processing contextual information in general.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison between the CFE experiment (Figure 3) and the neutral context control experiment (Figure 4).

claim: CFE-specific synaptic changes spread on RE+ dendrite beyond RE+ synapses, suggesting a more global impact of RE on synaptic plasticity in dCA1.
source: Moreover, as some CFE-specific synaptic changes spread on RE+ dendrite beyond RE+ synapses, our data suggest a more global impact of RE on synaptic plasticity in dCA1.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that RE+/- spines (on RE+ dendrites but not directly contacting RE axons) also showed CFE-induced changes (Figure 3D).

claim: The identification of RE- dendritic spines had only 68% accuracy due to 68% penetrance of mCherry AAV in RE.
source: We assume that the identification of RE- dendritic spines had only 68% accuracy due to 68% penetrance of mCherry AAV in RE (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the viral penetrance data.

claim: CFE induces the growth of SLM synapses.
source: Next, to verify whether CFE induces the growth of SLM synapses, we utilized SBFSEM.
evidence: The claim is tested using SBFSEM analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: The overall growth of SLM synapses should be detectable with SBFSEM as a consequence of the large structural and molecular alterations of RE+ dendrites that affected the global statistics.
source: Hence, we assumed that the overall growth of SLM synapses should be detectable also with SBFSEM as a consequence of the large structural and molecular alterations of RE+ dendrites that affected the global statistics.
evidence: The claim is based on the reasoning that RE+ dendrite changes were large enough to affect global measurements, as observed in confocal analysis (Figure 3D).

claim: 238 dendritic spines with PSDs were reconstructed from the brains of the mice sacrificed 24 hr after CFC (5US, n = 5).
source: In total, we reconstructed 238 dendritic spines with PSDs from the brains of the mice sacrificed 24 hr after CFC (5US, n = 5), 257 of the mice sacrificed after CFE session (Ext, n = 6), and 315 of the naive mice (Naive, n = 4).
evidence: The claim is based on SBFSEM reconstruction data.

claim: 257 dendritic spines with PSDs were reconstructed from the brains of the mice sacrificed after CFE session (Ext, n = 6).
source: In total, we reconstructed 238 dendritic spines with PSDs from the brains of the mice sacrificed 24 hr after CFC (5US, n = 5), 257 of the mice sacrificed after CFE session (Ext, n = 6), and 315 of the naive mice (Naive, n = 4).
evidence: The claim is based on SBFSEM reconstruction data.

claim: 315 dendritic spines with PSDs were reconstructed from the brains of naive mice (Naive, n = 4).
source: In total, we reconstructed 238 dendritic spines with PSDs from the brains of the mice sacrificed 24 hr after CFC (5US, n = 5), 257 of the mice sacrificed after CFE session (Ext, n = 6), and 315 of the naive mice (Naive, n = 4).
evidence: The claim is based on SBFSEM reconstruction data.

claim: Dendritic spine density did not differ between the experimental groups in SLM.
source: We found that dendritic spine density did not differ between the experimental groups (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by SBFSEM quantification shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Dendritic spine volume was bigger in the Ext group compared to the Naive and 5US animals in SLM.
source: However, dendritic spine volume, PSDs volume, and surface area were bigger in the Ext group compared to the Naive and 5US animals (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by SBFSEM quantification shown in Figure 5C.

claim: PSDs volume was bigger in the Ext group compared to the Naive and 5US animals in SLM.
source: However, dendritic spine volume, PSDs volume, and surface area were bigger in the Ext group compared to the Naive and 5US animals (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by SBFSEM quantification shown in Figure 5E.

claim: PSD surface area was bigger in the Ext group compared to the Naive and 5US animals in SLM.
source: However, dendritic spine volume, PSDs volume, and surface area were bigger in the Ext group compared to the Naive and 5US animals (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by SBFSEM quantification shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Dendritic spine volume, PSD volume, and PSD surface area were tightly correlated in all experimental groups.
source: These parameters were tightly correlated in all experimental groups.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: The lines describing the correlations in the Ext animals were slightly moved upward compared to the 5US group, indicating that during the CFE session PSDs increased in size more than dendritic spines.
source: However, the lines describing the correlations in the Ext animals were slightly moved upward compared to the 5US group, indicating that during the CFE session PSDs increased in size more than dendritic spines.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5D and E.

claim: Neither density of macular nor complex PSDs differed between the experimental groups in SLM.
source: Neither density of macular nor complex PSDs differed between the experimental groups.
evidence: The claim is supported by SBFSEM quantification shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: The volume of macular PSDs in the Ext group was significantly larger than in the 5US animals.
source: However, the volume of macular, but not complex, PSDs in the Ext group was significantly larger than in the 5US animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by SBFSEM quantification shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The volume of complex PSDs did not differ between Ext and 5US groups.
source: However, the volume of macular, but not complex, PSDs in the Ext group was significantly larger than in the 5US animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by SBFSEM quantification shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The volumes of PSDs of both categories were larger in the Ext group compared to naive animals.
source: The volumes of PSDs of both categories were larger in the Ext group compared to naive animals.
evidence: The claim is supported by SBFSEM quantification shown in Figure 5F and G.

claim: CFE results in the growth of SLM dendritic spines and excitatory synapses located on the spines, suggesting their strengthening.
source: Overall, SBFSEM analysis confirmed that CFE results in the growth of SLM dendritic spines and excitatory synapses located on the spines, suggesting their strengthening (Holtmaat and Svoboda, 2009; Patterson and Yasuda, 2011).
evidence: The claim is inferred from SBFSEM data showing increased spine and PSD volumes in the Ext group (Figure 5), and is supported by citations to literature linking structural changes to synaptic strengthening.

claim: Growth was observed in the category of small macular PSDs.
source: In particular, we observed growth in the category of small macular PSDs, possibly explaining how such synaptic changes could occur so rapidly.
evidence: The claim is supported by SBFSEM quantification showing increased volume of macular PSDs in the Ext group (Figure 5F).

claim: No volume changes were observed in complex PSDs in the Ext groups compared to the 5US animals possibly because large synapses are more stable.
source: No volume changes were observed in complex PSDs in the Ext groups compared to the 5US animals possibly because large synapses are more stable (Borczyk et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by SBFSEM data (Figure 5G) and a citation to literature on synapse stability.

claim: The analysis of dendritic spine volumes, as a proxy of synaptic changes, likely underestimates the actual changes of the synapses.
source: Importantly, our correlation analysis for PSDs and dendritic spines demonstrates that the analysis of dendritic spine volumes, as a proxy of synaptic changes, likely underestimates the actual changes of the synapses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that PSDs increased in size more than dendritic spines during CFE (Figure 5D, E).

claim: The hM4Di mice from the CNO group had higher levels of freezing compared to the saline animals during the CFE memory test.
source: The hM4Di mice from the CNO group had higher levels of freezing compared to the saline animals, suggesting impaired long-term CFE memory (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6D (unpaired t-test: t(20) = 3.26, p=0.002).

claim: No effect of CNO on freezing was observed in the control group during the CFE memory test.
source: We did not observe such an effect of CNO in the control group (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6E (unpaired t-test: t(10) = 0.149, p=0.884).

claim: The CNO group showed higher freezing levels both during a short-term (Test 1) and long-term CFE memory test (Extinction 2) compared to the saline animals.
source: However, the CNO group, compared to the saline animals, showed higher freezing levels both during a short-term (Test 1) and long-term CFE memory test (Extinction 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The CNO and saline groups showed no difference in freezing levels in the context B (CtxB).
source: They showed, however, no difference in freezing levels in the CtxB (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: RE→dCA1 regulates formation of short- and long-term CFE memory but not recognition of the training context.
source: Hence, our results indicate that RE→dCA1 regulates formation of short- and long-term CFE memory but not recognition of the training context.
evidence: The claim is inferred from behavioral data showing impaired CFE memory but no impairment in context discrimination after RE→dCA1 inhibition (Figure 6F).

claim: Mice injected with CNO showed higher freezing during the first 5 min of Extinction compared to the mice injected with saline in the hM4Di virus group.
source: In the hM4Di virus group, mice injected with CNO showed higher freezing during the first 5 min of Extinction compared to the mice injected with saline.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The hM4Di mice injected with CNO had higher levels of freezing compared to the mice injected with saline during the CFE memory test.
source: However, when CFE memory was tested (Test), the hM4Di mice injected with CNO had higher levels of freezing compared to the mice injected with saline.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6G (unpaired t-test, t(15) = 2.30. p=0.036).

claim: Freezing levels in the control CNO and saline groups differed neither during the CFC, nor during Extinction and Test.
source: Similarly, as in our former study (Tomaszewski et al., 2024), freezing levels in the control CNO and saline groups differed neither during the CFC, nor during Extinction and Test (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6H and a citation to a previous study.

claim: Transient inhibition of RE→dCA1 has no effect on working memory (changes of freezing behavior within CFE session) but impairs both short- and long-term CFE memory even after two CFE sessions.
source: Overall, these results indicate that transient inhibition of RE→dCA1 has no effect on working memory (changes of freezing behavior within CFE session) but impairs both short- and long-term CFE memory even after two CFE sessions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from behavioral data showing that CNO did not affect within-session extinction but impaired memory tested at later time points (Figure 6D, F, G).

claim: Transient inhibition of RE→dCA1 has no effect on contextual fear memory generalization.
source: We have also observed that it has no effect on contextual fear memory generalization but enhances contextual fear recall in mice that had CNO delivered to dCA1 through cannulas.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data showing no difference in freezing in context B between CNO and saline groups (Figure 6F).

claim: Inhibition of RE→dCA1 enhances contextual fear recall in mice that had CNO delivered to dCA1 through cannulas.
source: We have also observed that it has no effect on contextual fear memory generalization but enhances contextual fear recall in mice that had CNO delivered to dCA1 through cannulas.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data showing higher freezing during the first 5 min of extinction in CNO-treated mice with cannulas (Figure 6G).

claim: Cannulas implantation impaired memory formation, possibly due to damage to the cortex.
source: Interestingly, in the saline groups with cannulas, the freezing levels were lower compared to the control groups in the experiments without cannulas (58–62% vs. 68–83%) (Figure 6A and C), suggesting that cannulas implantation impaired memory formation, possibly due to damage to the cortex (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison of freezing levels between groups with and without cannulas.

claim: Inhibition of RE→dCA1 may enhance contextual fear recall only when the memory trace is suboptimal.
source: Hence, inhibition of RE→dCA1 may enhance contextual fear recall only when the memory trace is suboptimal (Figure 6G), while CFE is regulated by this pathway across many experimental conditions (Figure 6C, F and G).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that enhanced fear recall was only observed in mice with cannulas (which had lower baseline freezing) but not in intact mice.

claim: CFE is regulated by the RE→dCA1 pathway across many experimental conditions.
source: Hence, inhibition of RE→dCA1 may enhance contextual fear recall only when the memory trace is suboptimal (Figure 6G), while CFE is regulated by this pathway across many experimental conditions (Figure 6C, F and G).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the consistent observation of impaired CFE across multiple experimental manipulations (Figure 6C, F, G).

claim: PSD-95 levels were significantly lower in SLM in the hM4Di group treated with CNO compared to the control group treated with CNO and the hM4Di group treated with saline.
source: PSD-95 levels were significantly lower in SLM in the hM4Di group treated with CNO compared to the control group treated with CNO and the hM4Di group treated with saline (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: No differences in PSD-95 levels were observed in SO and SR after chemogenetic inhibition of RE.
source: Such differences were not observed in other strata.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of RE affected CFE-induced molecular changes of the excitatory synapses within RE input areas.
source: Hence, chemogenetic inhibition of RE affected CFE-induced molecular changes of the excitatory synapses within RE input areas, possibly affecting the integration of information from other regions involved in CFE (Baldi and Bucherelli, 2014; Baldi and Bucherelli, 2015; Bevilaqua et al., 2006; Ji and Maren, 2008; Cai et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that RE inhibition blocked CFE-induced PSD-95 changes in SLM (Figure 7D), and is supported by citations to literature on brain regions involved in CFE.

claim: RE, dCA1, and RE→CA1 projections are necessary for the formation and retrieval of fear extinction memories.
source: RE, dCA1, and RE→CA1 projections are necessary for the formation and retrieval of fear extinction memories (Venkataraman and Dias, 2023; Cassel et al., 2013; Totty et al., 2023; Ratigan et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In the SLM CFE upregulates the levels of synaptic scaffold protein, PSD-95.
source: Moreover, we discovered that in the SLM CFE upregulates the levels of synaptic scaffold protein, PSD-95 (Chen et al., 2011; El-Husseini et al., 2000; Kornau et al., 1995), accompanied by structural plasticity of RE→dCA1 synapses—growth of RE boutons and dendritic spines located on the RE+ dendrites.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3D and citations to literature on PSD-95.

claim: CFE is accompanied by structural plasticity of RE→dCA1 synapses—growth of RE boutons and dendritic spines located on the RE+ dendrites in SLM.
source: Moreover, we discovered that in the SLM CFE upregulates the levels of synaptic scaffold protein, PSD-95 (Chen et al., 2011; El-Husseini et al., 2000; Kornau et al., 1995), accompanied by structural plasticity of RE→dCA1 synapses—growth of RE boutons and dendritic spines located on the RE+ dendrites.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figures 2D and 3D.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of the RE→dCA1 pathway impaired CFE.
source: Finally, chemogenetic inhibition of the RE→dCA1 pathway impaired CFE, while chemogenetic inhibition of RE blocked the CFE-induced expression of PSD-95 in SLM.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of RE blocked the CFE-induced expression of PSD-95 in SLM.
source: Finally, chemogenetic inhibition of the RE→dCA1 pathway impaired CFE, while chemogenetic inhibition of RE blocked the CFE-induced expression of PSD-95 in SLM.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: The RE→SLM pathway participates in the updating of fearful context value by actively regulating CFE-induced molecular and structural synaptic plasticity in the SLM.
source: In summary, our observations support a framework in which the RE→SLM pathway participates in the updating of fearful context value by actively regulating CFE-induced molecular and structural synaptic plasticity in the SLM.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined observations of RE→SLM synaptic changes during CFE (Figures 2-5), impaired CFE after RE→dCA1 inhibition (Figure 6), and blocked PSD-95 changes after RE inhibition (Figure 7).

claim: RE projects to the hippocampal formation and forms asymmetric synapses with dendritic spines and dendrites, suggesting innervation of excitatory synapses on both excitatory and aspiny inhibitory neurons.
source: RE projects to the hippocampal formation and forms asymmetric synapses with dendritic spines and dendrites, suggesting innervation of excitatory synapses on both excitatory and aspiny inhibitory neurons (Wouterlood et al., 1990; Herkenham, 1978; Kajiwara et al., 2008; Vertes et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: RE modulates function of the pyramidal cells by monosynaptic excitatory and polysynaptic inhibitory mechanisms.
source: This conclusion was confirmed by the electrophysiological studies showing that RE modulates function of the pyramidal cells by monosynaptic excitatory and polysynaptic inhibitory mechanisms (Dolleman-Van der Weel et al., 1997; Kajiwara et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous electrophysiological studies.

claim: RE boutons were observed in close apposition to dCA1 dendritic spines containing PSD-95-positive puncta, confirming innervation of the pyramidal neurons via excitatory synapses.
source: Here, we observed RE boutons in close apposition to dCA1 dendritic spines containing PSD-95-positive puncta, confirming innervation of the pyramidal neurons via excitatory synapses.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The RE axons were found both in SO and SLM of dCA1, with the latter having much bigger boutons.
source: The RE axons were found both in SO and SLM of dCA1, with the latter having much bigger boutons (Figure 1A–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1.

claim: RE activity increases excitatory synaptic transmission both in SO and SLM.
source: Hence, our data supports the notion that RE activity increases excitatory synaptic transmission both in SO and SLM.
evidence: The claim is inferred from electrophysiological data showing that CNO-mediated inhibition of RE decreased fEPSP in SO and SLM (Figure 1J, L).

claim: The observation of RE axons in SO is surprising since RE projections were described so far only in SLM.
source: Since RE projections were described so far only in SLM, the observation of RE axons in SO is surprising.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with previous literature and the current findings.

claim: RE axons in SO are thinner and have much smaller boutons compared to SLM.
source: This discrepancy with former studies may stem from the fact that RE axons in SO are thinner and have much smaller boutons compared to SLM.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: RE axons in SO are clearly visible only with confocal imaging of high magnification (×100).
source: Hence, RE axons in SO are clearly visible only with confocal imaging of high magnification (×100, see Figure 1C vs. D).
evidence: The claim is based on methodological observations from the current study.

claim: Both formation and extinction of contextual fear memories involve structural synaptic plasticity in dCA1.
source: Both formation (Abraham et al., 2019; Bliss and Collingridge, 1993; Morris et al., 2003; Radwanska et al., 2011) and extinction of contextual fear memories (Ziółkowska et al., 2023; Schuette et al., 2020; Stansley et al., 2018; Garín-Aguilar et al., 2012) involve structural synaptic plasticity in dCA1.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Behavioral training may result in rapid (<45 min) synapse remodeling, synaptogenesis, and synapse elimination.
source: While most of the former studies focused on training-induced synaptic changes at more remote time points (>2 hr after training), some experiments have demonstrated that behavioral training may result in rapid (<45 min) synapse remodeling, synaptogenesis, and synapse elimination (Ziółkowska et al., 2023; Gipson et al., 2013a; Gipson et al., 2013b).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: 30-min-long CFE session induced structural synaptic plasticity in dCA1 pyramidal neurons in a stratum-specific manner.
source: In particular, we have previously demonstrated that 30-min-long CFE session induced structural synaptic plasticity in dCA1 pyramidal neurons in a stratum-specific manner, and it was accompanied by phosphorylation of PSD-95 at serine 73 and alterations of PSD-95 protein levels (Ziółkowska et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the same authors.

claim: Phosphorylation of PSD-95 at serine 73 in dCA1 is required for CFE and CFE-induced structural plasticity of SO synapses.
source: We also showed that phosphorylation of PSD-95 at serine 73 in dCA1 is required for CFE and CFE-induced structural plasticity of SO synapses.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the same authors (Ziółkowska et al., 2023).

claim: Rapid and PSD-95-dependent structural synaptic plasticity is an important step in the regulation of the dCA1 circuit during CFE.
source: Thus, rapid and PSD-95-dependent structural synaptic plasticity is an important step in the regulation of the dCA1 circuit during CFE.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the previous findings cited and the current observations.

claim: CFE-induced increase of PSD-95 levels per dendritic spine and morphological changes of dendritic spines occurred in SO and SLM, but not SR.
source: Here, we observed that CFE-induced increase of PSD-95 levels per dendritic spine and morphological changes of dendritic spines occurred in SO and SLM, but not SR, while the changes of dendritic spine density were observed only in SO.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The changes of dendritic spine density were observed only in SO.
source: Here, we observed that CFE-induced increase of PSD-95 levels per dendritic spine and morphological changes of dendritic spines occurred in SO and SLM, but not SR, while the changes of dendritic spine density were observed only in SO.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Coupling of PSD size to spine volume was assumed to be a permanent spine feature.
source: So far, coupling of PSD size to spine volume was assumed to be a permanent spine feature (Arellano et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Uncoupling of PSD and spine volumes was shown to be transient (<7 min) after glutamate uncaging and caused by slower growth of a PSD compared with a spine.
source: Uncoupling of PSD and spine volumes was shown to be transient (<7 min) after glutamate uncaging and caused by slower growth of a PSD compared with a spine (Bosch et al., 2014; Meyer et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PSD-core growth exceeds dendritic spine growth for at least 30 min.
source: Here, similarly as in our former studies (Ziółkowska et al., 2023; Borczyk et al., 2019; Śliwińska et al., 2020), we show that PSD-core growth exceeds dendritic spine growth for at least 30 min.
evidence: The claim is supported by SBFSEM data shown in Figure 5 and citations to previous studies by the same authors.

claim: Changes in the ratio between PSD-core volume and dendritic spine volume likely impact the stoichiometry between proteins in the PSD and those in the dendritic spine, influencing the properties of their complexes, long-term synaptic stability, synaptic strength, and dendritic spine sizes.
source: Changes in the ratio between these two compartments likely impact the stoichiometry between proteins in the PSD and those in the dendritic spine, influencing the properties of their complexes, long-term synaptic stability, synaptic strength, and dendritic spine sizes.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the functional consequences of the observed structural changes.

claim: CFE results in spinogenesis of RE+/+ spines and increased median size of RE boutons, RE+/+ and RE+/- spines in SLM.
source: In particular, CFE results in spinogenesis of RE+/+ spines and increased median size of RE boutons, RE+/+ and RE+/- spines in SLM.
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figures 2D and 3D.

claim: Former studies linked the behavioral functions of RE with its impact on the coherence of theta oscillations between the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex.
source: Thus, while former studies linked the behavioral functions of RE with its impact on the coherence of theta oscillations between the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex (Griffin, 2021; Totty et al., 2023; Ito et al., 2015), we extend these findings demonstrating the impact of RE on training-induced structural and molecular plasticity of the excitatory synapses in dCA1 that participates in CFE.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: RE has a very significant impact on dCA1 excitatory synapses despite RE+/+ dendritic spines being sparse in dCA1.
source: Although RE+/+ dendritic spines are sparse in dCA1 (based on mCherry AAV penetrance in RE and frequency of RE+/+ dendritic spines in our study, we asses that they constitute 5–6% of all synapses), our findings show that RE has a very significant impact on dCA1 excitatory synapses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that RE inhibition affects global PSD-95 levels in SLM (Figure 7) despite RE+/+ spines being only 5-6% of all synapses.

claim: Chemogenetic inhibition of RE prevents CFE-induced expression of PSD-95 globally in SLM.
source: In particular, we have observed that chemogenetic inhibition of RE prevents CFE-induced expression of PSD-95 globally in SLM, suggesting the effect of RE on dCA1 synapses that spreads far beyond RE+/+ inputs.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Differential CFE-induced structural synaptic plasticity was observed on RE+/- and RE-/- spines, suggesting heterosynaptic contribution of RE to plasticity of RE+/- dendritic spines.
source: Moreover, we observed differential CFE-induced structural synaptic plasticity on RE+/- and RE-/- spines, suggesting heterosynaptic contribution of RE to plasticity of RE+/- dendritic spines.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that RE+/- spines showed CFE-induced changes while RE- spines did not in SLM (Figure 3D).

claim: RE stimulation produced large negative-going field potentials at SLM, indicative of prominent depolarizing actions on distal apical dendrites of CA1 pyramidal cells.
source: In agreement with these findings, Dolleman-Van der Weel et al., 1997 demonstrated that RE stimulation produced large negative-going field potentials at SLM, indicative of prominent depolarizing actions on distal apical dendrites of CA1 pyramidal cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: RE may exert a persistent influence on the state of pyramidal cell excitability, depolarizing cells to close to threshold for activation by other excitatory inputs.
source: Hence, RE may exert a persistent influence on the state of pyramidal cell excitability, depolarizing cells to close to threshold for activation by other excitatory inputs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the cited electrophysiological findings and the current observations.

claim: RE actions on CA1 were in some cases considerably greater than those of CA3 on the CA1.
source: Consistent with this, Bertram and Zhang, 1999 compared the effects of stimulation of the RE with stimulation of the CA3 region of the hippocampus on population responses at CA1 and reported that RE actions on CA1 were in some cases considerably greater than those of CA3 on the CA1.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Intra-RE infusions of ketamine and muscimol bidirectionally regulate neuronal firing and delta power in CA1.
source: Moreover, intra-RE infusions of ketamine and muscimol bidirectionally regulate neuronal firing and delta power in CA1 (Zhang and Lisman, 2012; Duan et al., 2015; Roy et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: RE may impact general activity of CA1 neurons.
source: Altogether, this data indicates that RE may impact general activity of CA1 neurons.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the cited literature on RE's effects on CA1 activity.

claim: The regulation of synaptic protein expression, including PSD-95, beyond RE+/+ synapses is likely important.
source: Although the mechanism is poorly understood, the regulation of synaptic protein expression, including PSD-95, beyond RE+/+ synapses is likely important.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the functional significance of the observed widespread PSD-95 changes.

claim: The effects of RE on synaptic levels of PSD-95 may affect the integration of information from other dCA1 inputs that regulate CFE, such as the entorhinal cortex or CA3 area.
source: In addition, the effects of RE on synaptic levels of PSD-95 may affect the integration of information from other dCA1 inputs that regulate CFE, such as the entorhinal cortex or CA3 area (Baldi and Bucherelli, 2014; Baldi and Bucherelli, 2015; Bevilaqua et al., 2006; Ji and Maren, 2008; Cai et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by citations to literature on brain regions involved in CFE.

claim: Former studies demonstrated the role of the RE in fear memory encoding, retrieval, extinction, and generalization.
source: The former studies demonstrated the role of the RE in fear memory encoding, retrieval, extinction, and generalization (Ramanathan et al., 2018; Xu and Südhof, 2013; Troyner and Bertoglio, 2021; Ramanathan and Maren, 2019; Vasudevan et al., 2022; Vetere et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Recent work has shown the role of the RE→dCA1 pathway in extinction of contextual fear and recall of CFE.
source: Furthermore, recent work has shown the role of the RE→dCA1 pathway in extinction of contextual fear and recall of CFE (Totty et al., 2023; Ratigan et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Transient chemogenetic inhibition of RE→dCA1 during the first fear extinction session resulted in impaired extinction not only during the short- and long-term CFE memory test but also throughout the entire second extinction session.
source: In addition, we observed that transient chemogenetic inhibition of RE→dCA1 during the first fear extinction session resulted in impaired extinction not only during the short- and long-term CFE memory test but also throughout the entire second extinction session.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: This persistent impairment of CFE alludes to long-term extinction impairment induced by PSD-95 mutation in dCA1 observed in a former study.
source: This persistent impairment of CFE alludes to long-term extinction impairment induced by PSD-95 mutation in dCA1 observed in our former study.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with a previous study by the same authors.

claim: Contextual fear memory cannot be updated by the animals with dCA1 phosphorylation-deficient PSD-95(S73A) mutation even if they undergo six 30 min CFE sessions.
source: We found that contextual fear memory cannot be updated by the animals with dCA1 phosphorylation-deficient PSD-95(S73A) mutation even if they undergo six 30 min CFE sessions (Ziółkowska et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study by the same authors.

claim: CFE-induced and PSD-95-dependent synaptic plasticity in dCA1 is necessary to reconsolidate and link the memories of contextual fear and CFE in order to persistently suppress contextual fear.
source: Hence, our data support the framework in which CFE-induced and PSD-95-dependent synaptic plasticity in dCA1 is necessary to reconsolidate and link the memories of contextual fear and CFE in order to persistently suppress contextual fear.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the current findings and previous work on PSD-95's role in CFE.

claim: The need for interaction between contextual fear and CFE memory traces for fear extinction to occur, and the contribution of RE in this process, was also suggested by Totty et al., 2023.
source: The need for interaction between these two memory traces for fear extinction to occur, and the contribution of RE in this process, was also suggested by Totty et al., 2023.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The RE-regulated synaptic alterations of PSD-95 levels that spread far beyond RE+/+ synapses may facilitate integration of contextual fear and CFE information that are likely generated by different dCA1 inputs.
source: The RE-regulated synaptic alterations of PSD-95 levels that spread far beyond RE+/+ synapses may facilitate integration of contextual fear and CFE information that are likely generated by different dCA1 inputs (Baldi and Bucherelli, 2014; Baldi and Bucherelli, 2015; Bevilaqua et al., 2006; Ji and Maren, 2008; Cai et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by citations to literature on brain regions involved in CFE.

claim: The integration of all inputs to dCA1, conveying different aspects of the cognitive process, is required for optimal extinction of contextual fear.
source: Thus, we assume that the integration of all inputs to dCA1, conveying different aspects of the cognitive process (Baldi and Bucherelli, 2015; Bevilaqua et al., 2006), is required for optimal extinction of contextual fear.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by citations to literature.

claim: Previous work has found that RE is necessary for proper discrimination of contexts.
source: Previous work has found that RE is necessary for proper discrimination of contexts (Xu and Südhof, 2013), and reductions in context discrimination might result in a relapse of fear (Bouton and Bolles, 1979).

claim: Reductions in context discrimination might result in a relapse of fear.
source: Previous work has found that RE is necessary for proper discrimination of contexts (Xu and Südhof, 2013), and reductions in context discrimination might result in a relapse of fear (Bouton and Bolles, 1979).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The activity of RE axons in CA1 is not contextually modulated.
source: However, more recent studies showed that the activity of RE axons in CA1 is not contextually modulated (Ratigan et al., 2023) and that 8 Hz stimulation of RE does not impair context recognition, although it affects recall of CFE (Totty et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: 8 Hz stimulation of RE does not impair context recognition, although it affects recall of CFE.
source: However, more recent studies showed that the activity of RE axons in CA1 is not contextually modulated (Ratigan et al., 2023) and that 8 Hz stimulation of RE does not impair context recognition, although it affects recall of CFE (Totty et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: No significant changes of RE+/+ synapses were observed upon exposure to neutral context.
source: We also see neither significant changes of RE+/+ synapses upon exposure to neutral context nor impairments of context recognition after chemogenetic inhibition of RE→CA1.

claim: No impairments of context recognition were observed after chemogenetic inhibition of RE→CA1.
source: We also see neither significant changes of RE+/+ synapses upon exposure to neutral context nor impairments of context recognition after chemogenetic inhibition of RE→CA1.

claim: Impaired fear extinction upon RE inactivation is a result of deficits in memory integration, rather than impaired recognition of the extinction context.
source: Hence, our work supports the notion that impaired fear extinction upon RE inactivation is a result of deficits in memory integration, rather than impaired recognition of the extinction context.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that RE→CA1 inhibition impaired CFE but not context recognition.

claim: This study illustrates a novel synaptic mechanism that participates in updating of contextual fear memories.
source: Overall, our study illustrates a novel synaptic mechanism that participates in updating of contextual fear memories.
evidence: The claim is based on the overall findings of the study.

claim: This mechanism involves structural and molecular synaptic plasticity of the RE→dCA1 projections as well as global changes of PSD-95 levels in dCA1 area.
source: This mechanism involves structural and molecular synaptic plasticity of the RE→dCA1 projections as well as global changes of PSD-95 levels in dCA1 area.

claim: Memories may be repeatedly reorganized upon recall.
source: Since memories may be repeatedly reorganized upon recall (Nader et al., 2000; Schafe et al., 2001), the molecular and cellular mechanisms involved in extinction of the existing fearful, aversive, or appetitive memories provide excellent targets for memory impairment therapies.

claim: The molecular and cellular mechanisms involved in extinction of the existing fearful, aversive, or appetitive memories provide excellent targets for memory impairment therapies.
source: Since memories may be repeatedly reorganized upon recall (Nader et al., 2000; Schafe et al., 2001), the molecular and cellular mechanisms involved in extinction of the existing fearful, aversive, or appetitive memories provide excellent targets for memory impairment therapies.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation supported by citations to literature on memory reconsolidation.

claim: Understanding the mechanisms that underlie CFE may be relevant for post-traumatic stress disorder treatment.
source: In particular, understanding the mechanisms that underlie CFE may be relevant for post-traumatic stress disorder treatment.
evidence: The claim is based on speculation about the clinical relevance of the findings.

claim: Impairments in context-dependent behaviors have been associated with pathological conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder, schizophrenia, and substance use disorders.
source: Impairments in context-dependent behaviors have been associated with pathological conditions such as post-traumatic stress disorder, schizophrenia, and substance use disorders (Lissek et al., 2014; Garfinkel et al., 2014; Grodin et al., 2018; Maren et al., 2013).

claim: Understanding the molecular and cellular mechanisms that underlie the updating of contextual memories is crucial for developing new therapeutic approaches to alleviate persistent and unmalleable contextual fear or compulsive context-induced drug seeking.
source: Therefore, understanding the molecular and cellular mechanisms that underlie the updating of contextual memories is crucial for developing new therapeutic approaches to alleviate persistent and unmalleable contextual fear or compulsive context-induced drug seeking (Ji and Maren, 2007; Maren and Quirk, 2004; Myers and Davis, 2002).

claim: One way to study contextual memories in the laboratory animals is through contextual fear conditioning (CFC).
source: One way to study contextual memories in the laboratory animals is through contextual fear conditioning (CFC) (Maren et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature and is based on established knowledge.

claim: In CFC, a spatial context, referred to as the conditioned stimulus (CS), is repeatedly paired with a noxious unconditioned stimulus (US), typically a mild shock.
source: In CFC, a spatial context, referred to as the conditioned stimulus (CS), is repeatedly paired with a noxious unconditioned stimulus (US), typically a mild shock.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about CFC paradigm.

claim: Freezing behavior serves as a quantifiable measure of contextual fear memory.
source: Freezing behavior serves as a quantifiable measure of contextual fear memory.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about behavioral measures in fear conditioning.

claim: With continued exposure to the CS in the absence of the US, freezing behavior generally decreases and exploratory behavior increases.
source: With continued exposure to the CS in the absence of the US, freezing behavior generally decreases and exploratory behavior increases.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about extinction learning.

claim: This process is termed contextual fear extinction (CFE) and occurs as animals learn over time that the context no longer predicts shocks.
source: This process is termed contextual fear extinction (CFE) and occurs as animals learn over time that the context no longer predicts shocks.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about extinction learning.

claim: For extinction to take place, mice must actively recall and update contextual memories.
source: For extinction to take place, mice must actively recall and update contextual memories.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about extinction learning.

claim: The classic neuronal circuit of CFE includes medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), amygdala, and hippocampus.
source: The classic neuronal circuit of CFE includes medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), amygdala, and hippocampus (Maren et al., 2013; Orsini and Maren, 2012).

claim: Nucleus reuniens (RE), a ventral midline thalamic nucleus, sends axon collaterals to mPFC and the hippocampal CA1 area.
source: In particular, nucleus reuniens (RE), a ventral midline thalamic nucleus, sends axon collaterals to mPFC and the hippocampal CA1 area (Hoover and Vertes, 2012; Varela et al., 2014; Vertes et al., 2007; Goswamee et al., 2021; Dolleman-Van der Weel et al., 1997; Wouterlood et al., 1990), forming a disynaptic link that can coordinate neural activity between the two structures (Jayachandran et al., 2023; Dolleman-van der Weel et al., 2019; Griffin, 2021; Totty et al., 2023).

claim: RE forms a disynaptic link that can coordinate neural activity between mPFC and hippocampus.
source: In particular, nucleus reuniens (RE), a ventral midline thalamic nucleus, sends axon collaterals to mPFC and the hippocampal CA1 area (Hoover and Vertes, 2012; Varela et al., 2014; Vertes et al., 2007; Goswamee et al., 2021; Dolleman-Van der Weel et al., 1997; Wouterlood et al., 1990), forming a disynaptic link that can coordinate neural activity between the two structures (Jayachandran et al., 2023; Dolleman-van der Weel et al., 2019; Griffin, 2021; Totty et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Activity-dependent brain mapping studies have revealed increased cfos expression in the RE following CFE learning and recall.

claim: Activity of RE is synchronized with freezing bouts.
source: Activity of RE is synchronized with freezing bouts (Silva et al., 2021; Ratigan et al., 2023), suggesting that activity patterns in the RE are related to the suppression of fear responses.

claim: Activity patterns in the RE are related to the suppression of fear responses.
source: Activity of RE is synchronized with freezing bouts (Silva et al., 2021; Ratigan et al., 2023), suggesting that activity patterns in the RE are related to the suppression of fear responses.

claim: Muscimol-induced inactivation of RE following a weak fear conditioning procedure enhances fear memory consolidation.
source: Indeed, muscimol-induced inactivation of RE following a weak fear conditioning procedure enhances fear memory consolidation (Troyner et al., 2018).
